query: For high-entropy alloys intended for thermal-insulation or radiation-resistant applications, what single intervention could reduce phonon thermal conductivity? Formulate one testable hypothesis that specifies the intervention, the physical mechanism, the predicted change relative to an otherwise comparable untreated alloy, the temperature and material-state boundaries over which it should hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment whose result would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing porosity into high-entropy alloys can reduce phonon thermal conductivity due to enhanced phonon scattering.
generation.mechanism: derived from materials-science principles, as phonon scattering is enhanced by the introduction of porosity, leading to reduced thermal conductivity
generation.boundary: temperature range from room temperature to high temperatures
generation.uncertainty: exact amount of reduction in thermal conductivity depends on porosity level and distribution

falsification_experiment.design: measure thermal conductivity of high-entropy alloy with and without porosity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: if thermal conductivity is not reduced with introduction of porosity, hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: This work shed light on the effect of constituent elements on local chemical fluctuation and lattice thermal conductivity in high-entropy thermoelectric materials and also revealed the direct relationship between the fluctuation and atomic characteristic of elements, which could serve as a guide for tailoring local chemical fluctuation in the community of high-entropy materials.

The term “high-entropy alloy” was introduced by Yeh et al. in 2004 [,]. The multiple principal elements in HEAs, especially those with significant atomic radius differences, cause lattice distortion []. The lattice distortion and inherent chemical disorder of HEAs lead to fluctuations in interatomic force constants and mass, resulting in intensified anharmonic phonon-phonon interactions [] and a reduced lattice thermal conductivity. Studies have shown that HEAs exhibit semimetallic characteristics, where the contribution of phonons to heat conduction can be comparable to that of electrons []. Moreover, charge carriers can move freely when the phonons are hindered and scattered, which is beneficial for achieving a high ZT (thermoelectric figure of merit) value as well as a high efficiency in thermal-energy management []. These features suggest that HEAs are potential next-generation thermoelectric materials. Therefore, researching the thermal physical properties and heat transfer mechanisms of HEAs is of great significance. Recently, a new family of compositionally complex (containing 4, 5, or more elements) but structurally simple (e.g. face center cubic - FCC structured) alloys, such as high-entropy alloys (HEA), has been successfully fabricated, in which the atomic fraction of each component is equal or near-equal. Therefore, the knowledge obtained from traditional solid solution alloys with distinguishable “solvent” and “solute” species may not be suitable to describe those alloys, and their mechanical and physical properties may be unique with potential practical applications. For example, in contrast to most traditional materials in which an inverse temperature-dependence of strength and ductility is usually observed, recent mechanical testing has shown that the FCC NiCoFeCrMn HEA shows simultaneous increases in both strength and ductility with decreasing test temperature (e.g. from 293 to 77 K). This alloy also has excellent fracture toughness at liquid nitrogen temperature, as high as 200 MPa m1/2, which is comparable to the very best cryogenic steels.
